growth_story.headline: Guinea's income per person grew faster from 2016 on a bauxite boom; Simandou iron ore now opens a second boom, with weak links to jobs beyond mining.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2015, income per person in Guinea grew by 1.2 percent a year on average, and by 1.4 in the decade to 2015. That era ended with the Ebola epidemic, which the IMF says, along with political uncertainty and falling commodity prices, stalled activity in 2014 and 2015. Growth then jumped to 8.0 percent in 2016 and 7.5 in 2017, and averaged 3.9 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, as bauxite output surged and mining exports drove the economy. Investment swung widely, from 52.4 percent of GDP in 2016 to 15.0 in 2021 and back to 38.1 in 2025, while the Simandou iron ore project was being built. Income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, after growth of 5.0 percent that year, and Simandou began exporting iron ore in November 2025.

threads.title: Bauxite carries the boom
threads.text: Bauxite exports surged after 2016 and have carried growth since; the World Bank says mining also led growth in 2025. Total output grew much faster than income per person because the population grew fast too.

threads.title: Simandou opens a second boom
threads.text: Iron ore exports from Simandou began in November 2025, with the first large shipments in the first half of 2026. The World Bank calls this the start of a second mining boom and a third major commodity export.

threads.title: Weak links beyond mining
threads.text: Mining buys little from local firms and has few links to the rest of the economy. The World Bank ties the fall in non-mining exports since 2016 to a rising real exchange rate, and says mining-led growth has not brought broad gains in jobs.

citations.title: Guinea: Macro Poverty Outlook, October 2026
citations.quote: Limited local procurement, shallow downstream linkages, and a narrow domestic supply base hinder the transmission of mining booms into broad-based employment in labor-intensive sectors.

citations.title: Guinea Economic Update: Natural Resource Management for Development (First Edition)
citations.quote: Non-mining exports have declined in absolute terms since 2016, suggestive of ‘Dutch disease’, whereby REER appreciation makes Guinean non-mining exports more expensive

citations.title: Guinea Economic Update 2026: Beyond Mining - Turning Resource Wealth into Private Sector Growth and Job Creation
citations.quote: Mining-led growth does not automatically translate into more economic opportunities for the population.

threads.title: Ebola and a commodity slump
threads.text: Just before the bauxite boom, the Ebola epidemic of 2014 and 2015, political uncertainty and falling commodity prices brought activity to a halt, the IMF reported in 2016.

citations.title: Guinea: Sixth and Seventh Reviews under the Extended Credit Facility Arrangement (IMF Country Report No. 16/95)
citations.quote: Economic activity stalled as political uncertainty and the drop in commodity prices exacerbated the effects of the Ebola disease

since_last_year.text: Simandou began exporting iron ore in November 2025, adding a third major mining export alongside bauxite and gold. In the first half of 2026, the World Bank reports, inflation picked up on food prices, and in August 2026 the IMF reached a staff-level agreement with Guinea on a new loan program, saying growth is expected to speed up as mining output rises.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank's October 2026 note puts growth in income per person over 2016 to 2025 well above the 3.9 percent a year in this data. And the IMF described close to zero growth in 2014 and 2015, while this data shows income per person still rising by 1.2 percent in each of those years.
